text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

R. v. Johnson
,

2024 BCSC 2669

Date: 20241112

Docket:
187392-2

Registry: Victoria

Rex

v.

Christopher Sura Johnson

Before: The Honourable Justice Morley

Oral Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Crown:

T.P.
Stokes

Counsel for the Accused:

J.M.P.
Firestone

Place and Dates of Trial/Hearing:

Victoria,
B.C.

October
16 - 18, 2024

November
12, 2024

Place and Date of Judgment:

Victoria,
B.C.

November 12, 2024

[
1
]

THE COURT:
These
are oral reasons for judgment. If a transcript is ordered, I reserve the right
to edit it for errors, omissions, repetition, and clarity. The result will not
change, nor will the basis for it.

[
2
]

Christopher Sura Johnson is charged with the
following:

a)         one count of using or threatening to use a weapon in
committing an assault, contrary to
s. 267
(a) of the
Criminal Code
, and

b)         one count of operating a conveyance in a manner that,
having regard to all the circumstances, was dangerous to the public, contrary
to s. 320.13 of the
Code
.

[
3
]

Both counts arise out of an incident occurring
around 2:15 p.m. on December 3, 2023, in which Mr. Johnson's car almost
hit the complainant, Omar Babili.

[
4
]

The incident occurred at the west entrance to
the front driveway of the B.C. Legislature, at the intersection of Menzies and
Quebec Streets here in Victoria. I will refer to the space where the front
driveway, which extends north of the Legislative buildings, across the grounds,
intersects with the Menzies Street sidewalk as “the Driveway”. The Driveway, in
this narrow sense, is normally separated from the rest of the front driveway
running across the Legislative grounds by four bollards, to which staff have
keys. The bollards were in place at the time of the incident, so the driveway
was functionally part of the eastern sidewalk of Menzies Street.

[
5
]

Mr. Babili was a participant in, and marshal for,
a rally held on the front lawn of the Provincial Legislature, to protest the
actions of the Israeli government in Gaza, in the wake of the events of October
7, 2023. Mr. Johnson had stopped his car before the crosswalk that goes from
the corner of Menzies Street and Quebec Street to the northern end of the
driveway. Immediately before the incident, he was engaged in a heated argument
with another individual attending the rally, Ali Abou Said. As Mr. Babili
walked across Menzies Street to the driveway, he had a moment of eye contact
with Mr. Johnson. Mr. Babili waved the Palestinian flag and shouted “Free
Palestine.” Mr. Johnson then executed a sharp, sudden, and unexpected left turn
into the driveway, which I will refer to in these reasons as the “Sudden Left Turn”.
Mr. Babili ran out of the way. Mr. Johnson immediately got out of his car and
angrily confronted Mr. Abou Said.

[
6
]

The main issues in this trial are:

a)         With respect to the charge of assault with a weapon,
whether the Crown has proven beyond a reasonable doubt the necessary intent. As
I will explain later, this intent could either be to try to hit Mr. Babili or
to try to scare him by making him believe that he would be hit and would have
to run out of the way.

b)         With respect to the dangerous driving charge, whether the
Crown has established beyond a reasonable doubt the necessary marked departure
from the standard of care which a reasonable driver would have exercised in the
circumstances.

Evidence

[
7
]

Crown called three witnesses: Mr. Abou Said, Mr.
Babili, and Constable Nicholas Ross of the Legislative Assembly Protective Service.
Mr. Johnson testified in his own defence.

[
8
]

Mr. Abou Said is a 29-year-old accountant living
in Victoria. He is of Palestinian descent and grew up in Lebanon. Mr. Abou Said
testified that he first came into contact with Mr. Johnson when he heard him
yelling at the occupants of a van or truck decorated with a billboard calling
for free Palestine. Mr. Abou Said tried to get Mr. Johnson to move along. Mr.
Johnson's attention turned to Mr. Abou Said, and he began yelling at him. Mr. Abou
Said witnessed what I have referred to as the Sudden Left Turn. On
cross-examination, Mr. Abou Said acknowledged that he could not very accurately
estimate how fast Mr. Johnson's vehicle was going or how close it came to Mr.
Babili.

[
9
]

Mr. Babili is a 26-year-old civil engineering
student at UVic, currently living in Vancouver. He explained that the
organizers of the rally asked for individuals to volunteer as marshals, with a
responsibility to ensure the rally occurred safely and peacefully, and to
interact with the police. He volunteered to act in this capacity, and was
wearing a reflective vest identifying himself as such. He testified that while
he was walking to where his car was, in order to renew his parking ticket, he
heard a commotion which turned out to be Mr. Johnson arguing with Mr. Abou Said.
He recounted seeing Mr. Johnson, saying “Free Palestine,” Mr. Johnson's car
accelerating at him, and having to run to get out of the way. Mr. Babili
testified that he was traumatized by what happened.

[
10
]

On cross-examination, Mr. Babili also acknowledged that his
estimates of speed and distance of the car, from him, were not precise. In
direct examination, he said he distinctly heard Mr. Johnson's car “rev” its
engine, but in cross-examination agreed that he did not hear a distinct revving
independent of the acceleration that could also be heard, as I will note, in a
video that documented the event.

[
11
]

The third Crown witness was Constable Nicholas Ross, of the
Legislative Assembly Protective Services. Constable Ross was formerly a
sergeant with the Saanich Police Department. He also observed the Sudden Left Turn,
although from further away. Realizing that the situation was escalating, he
intervened and came between Mr. Johnson and Mr. Abou Said. He recounted what he
heard Mr. Johnson say to Mr. Abou Said, afterwards.

[
12
]

Mr. Johnson also testified. He is an apprentice carpenter, living in
Victoria. On December 3, 2023, he was planning to meet a friend at the Grand
Pacific Hotel. When he turned onto Menzies Street to get to the hotel's
parking, he noticed a truck or van with “Free Palestine” signs and decided to “lip
off” the occupants of the truck or van. He then discussed his initial
confrontation with Mr. Abou Said, the Sudden Left Turn, his subsequent argument
with Mr. Abou Said, Constable Ross's intervention, and his arrest.

[
13
]

Mr. Johnson conceded that he saw Mr. Babili before he made the Sudden
Left Turn. He forcefully denied that he intended to
hit
Mr. Babili. As I
will address in more detail, his answers as to whether he intended to
intimidate

or
threaten
Mr. Babili were more equivocal.

[
14
]

In addition, four videos were put into evidence:

a)         The first is a 56-second video from perspective of the
grounds on the Legislature, to the east of where the incident happened. I will
refer to this as Video 1. Video 1 has audio.

b)         The second was a 26‑second video taken by occupants
of a car parked on the west side of Menzies, two car lengths north of where Mr. Johnson's
vehicle was stopped prior to his turn. This is Video 2. Video 2 also has audio.

c)         The third is a four-minute video taken by a camera
mounted on the West Annex building of the Legislative precinct. I refer to this
as Video 3. Video 3 does not have audio, but does provide the most comprehensive
visual of the events.

d)         The fourth is a 27-second video taken from a camera
mounted at the middle front steps, near the formal entrance to the main
building of the Legislative precinct, Video 4. Video 4 has time stamps. Video 4
does not have audio. Video 4 is primarily useful for identifying the exact
times at which events occurred.

[
15
]

Given how important the videos are to reconstructing what happened,
I will briefly address the principles for making evidentiary findings from
videos. Once it is established that a video has not been altered or changed and
that it depicts the scene of an alleged crime, it becomes admissible and
relevant evidence:
R. v. Nikolovski
,
1996 CanLII 158 (SCC)
,
[1996] 3 S.C.R. 1197
at para.
28
.
It is agreed that the videos here have not been altered and depict a relevant
scene; the videos thus provide valuable evidence of what happened when Mr.
Johnson made the Sudden Left Turn into the driveway. I am mindful that as trier
of fact I must be careful in weighing video evidence, as in any other kind of
evidence, employing common sense, logic, and experience. I am aware that I
should not try to come to conclusions from video evidence that appropriately
require expert interpretation, none of which has been proffered as evidence here.
As trier of fact, I must also consider whether particular perspectives from
which videos were taken could lead to a misleading picture of events.

[
16
]

In argument, Mr. Firestone pointed out on behalf of Mr. Johnson that
the Crown has submitted no accident reconstruction evidence. Constable Ross,
based on his prior experience as a Saanich Police Department sergeant, agreed
with Mr. Firestone that such evidence is often called in dangerous driving
prosecutions. Obviously, to the extent the lack of evidence leaves reasonable
doubt on any factual point, the benefit of that doubt accrues to the accused. At
the same time, there is no absolute prerequisite that a particular type of
evidence be called in relation to any particular offence. Whether the elements
of the offence have been proven beyond a reasonable doubt has to be determined after
considering the totality of the evidence that is in fact submitted. I accept
that none of the eyewitnesses could reliably give precise speeds or distances,
but, as I will discuss, the Crown's case does not depend on the precision of
any eye witness' estimate in that regard. I also accept that I must be cautious
in making such inferences from the videos, and restrict myself to those can be
made on common sense and ordinary experience, as opposed to expert analysis.

Background Facts

[
17
]

With important exceptions, the witnesses largely agreed about the
sequence of events, and the videos provide the basis for an undisputed
chronology. I will begin by setting out what I take to be these undisputed
facts. This is intended to be a discussion of facts that were either agreed to
or with respect to which there was no conflict in the evidence. In any event, I
find no reason to doubt that these facts occurred as I will set them out. I
will later analyze conflicts in the evidence or inferences I am asked to make
with respect to the essential elements of the offence after reviewing the
substantive law in relation to the two offences and the principles binding on
me as trier of fact in a criminal trial.

[
18
]

On the afternoon of December 3, 2023, a rally was held on the front
lawn of the Provincial Legislature to protest the actions of the Israeli
government and the Israeli Defense Force in the Gaza Strip after the October 7,
2023 attack by Hamas, and allied paramilitaries in Israel. The official start
of the rally was 2 p.m. As I have mentioned, Mr. Babili had volunteered to act
as a marshal for the rally. His role was to keep participants safe and interact
with the police if anything happened. Mr. Abou Said was another rally
participant. They did not know each other at the time.

[
19
]

Mr. Johnson had planned to meet a friend that day at the Hotel Grand
Pacific, which is located a block to the west of the Legislature. He drove
there in his gray or silver 2006 Nissan Sentra SE4. As it happens, he is a
political activist and sympathetic to the Israeli side of the Gaza conflict,
but he was not aware that there was a rally occurring at the Legislature, until
he drove by it for unrelated reasons. However, when Mr. Johnson turned left from
Belleville Street, which runs between the Legislature lawn and the Inner
Harbor, onto Menzies Street, and he noticed a van or truck with signboards
prominently displaying the slogans, “Free Palestine” and “Boycott Israeli Apartheid”,
he decided to get into an argument.

[
20
]

Mr. Johnson stopped his car in the middle of the street and began
yelling at the occupants of the truck/van. The exact content of what he yelled
is disputed, and in any event not material. By Mr. Johnson's own account, it was
intended to be demeaning and degrading and involved comparing Palestine and
Palestinians to male genitalia.

[
21
]

Mr. Abou Said, who had drifted over from the main rally site in
front of the Legislature to Menzies Street to take a photo of the truck/van,
saw Mr. Johnson yelling at the occupants of the truck/van. Mr. Abou Said
characterized them as an older couple. He decided to try to get Mr. Johnson to
move on. Mr. Abou Said yelled, “Keep going” to Mr. Johnson, and repeated this
at least once.

[
22
]

This had the effect of causing Mr. Johnson to turn his attention to
Mr. Abou Said. In order to engage Mr. Abou Said directly, he pulled his car
forward a few meters so that it was just south of the crosswalk traversing
Menzies near Quebec Street. According to Video 3, he remained stopped there for
about 15 seconds, while he yelled at Mr. Abou Said. From the audio of Videos 1
and 2, I can tell that Mr. Johnson said something about the slogan “from the
river to the sea” and something about Jordan. Mr. Johnson testified that he was
aggressively confronting Mr. Abou Said, “lipping him off,” and that he yelled
insults associating Palestine and Palestinians with male genitals. Mr. Abou
Said testified, and it is confirmed by Video 2, that he responded by
saying, “Free Palestine.”

[
23
]

At this moment, Mr. Babili was returning from going to renew his
parking ticket, to see what the commotion was about. He crossed from the west
side of Menzies Street to the Legislature side, a little to the south of Quebec
Street, walking in a diagonal towards the area I have defined as “the Driveway”.
As Mr. Babili reached the Driveway, he turned toward Mr. Johnson, and they had
a moment of eye contact. Mr. Babili waved his flag and shouted “Free Palestine”.
Mr. Johnson then executed what I have referred to as the Sudden Left Turn.

[
24
]

Since the exact facts about the Sudden Left Turn and what they
demonstrate about Mr. Johnson's state of mind are at the heart of this case, I
will leave an extended discussion of it until later.

[
25
]

In any event, there is no controversy that after the Sudden Left Turn,
Mr. Johnson got out of his car, now parked on the Driveway, and walked
toward Mr. Abou Said to confront him. Mr. Abou Said took a few steps
towards Mr. Johnson. Mr. Johnson then stood toe to toe with Mr. Abou Said,
clearly in his personal space. The audio from Video 1 provides a clear record
of what Mr. Johnson and Mr. Abou Said said to each other, with some exceptions,
where I will note that what was said was inaudible.

[
26
]

As Mr. Johnson emerged from his car and walked toward Mr. Abou Said,
he yelled, “Who wants to go, right?” Once Mr. Johnson reached the space right
in front of Mr. Abou Said's space, he shouted, “They [presumably the Israelis]
have every right to that land. From the River to the Sea, eh? That’s what they
[presumably Palestinians and their supporters] said since ’48 [i.e., 1948, the
date of the founding of the state of Israel].”

[
27
]

To this, Mr. Abou Said responded, “And?” Mr. Johnson then said, “So,
when are you going to get the fucking reality? Go back to Jordan.”

[
28
]

The video shows that Constable Ross then stepped between Mr. Johnson
and Mr. Abou Said and attempted to de-escalate. He said to both men, “Step back.
This is an emotional situation.” Mr. Abou Said responded to this; he appears to
have objected to the characterization as suggesting a false equivalence between
what Mr. Johnson had done and Mr. Abou Said's reaction. Since Mr. Abou
Said was speaking more quietly than Mr. Johnson and there were other audible
reactions caught on the video, it is difficult to be clear what Mr. Abou Said
said. In any event, he was clearly trying to be as calm as possible in the
circumstances.

[
29
]

Mr. Johnson, although perhaps calming a bit as a result of Constable
Ross's presence, continued to yell. He stated, “These guys are a terrorist
organization” or perhaps “terrorist organizations.” He then repeated the phrase

terrorist organization
or
organizations
.

[
30
]

The interpretation of what Mr. Johnson said next is disputed and
extremely material. Video 1 shows that after saying “terrorist organization” (or
“terrorist organizations”) the second time, and as Constable Ross was moving
him slowly away, Mr. Johnson again faced Mr. Abou Said and said “Did you see
what I did just there,” pointing just in front of his car where Mr. Babili had
been at the time of the Sudden Left Turn. A male voice, not that of Mr. Abou
Said, Mr. Babili, or Constable Ross can be heard saying “That's against the law,”
and Mr. Johnson yelled, “That is what you're” (or possibly “they're”) “doing to
Jews all the time.”

[
31
]

Constable Ross used his physical presence to get Mr. Johnson to step
back further. Members of the Victoria Police Department arrived on the scene. Mr. Johnson
directed at Mr. Abou Said what I would call the “I am watching you” gesture, in
which he took his middle and index fingers to each of his eyes, and then
pointed them at Mr. Abou Said.

[
32
]

The Victoria Police Department then arrested Mr. Johnson.

Submissions of the Parties

[
33
]

Mr. Firestone submits, on Mr. Johnson's behalf, that there is a
reasonable doubt with respect to both counts of the indictment.

[
34
]

With respect to the assault with a weapon offence, he notes that
this is a specific intent offence, which can only be made out if the accused
had the intention to use his or her vehicle as a weapon. He argues that all of
the evidence is consistent with Mr. Johnson's focus being on Mr. Abou Said, not
Mr. Babili, and that Mr. Johnson's evidence that he did not intend to hit Mr.
Babili should be accepted, or at minimum raises a reasonable doubt as to whether
he had the necessary intent.

[
35
]

With respect to the dangerous driving offence, Mr. Firestone
concedes that if Mr. Johnson intended to hit Mr. Babili, this would amount to a
marked departure from the standard of care of the reasonable driver that would
constitute dangerous driving. However, he says that there is a reasonable
inference from the evidence that this was in fact a case of momentary
inattention, which might be the basis for civil negligence, but not of a kind
that is, “sufficiently egregious, in all the circumstances, to warrant
criminalization”:
R. v. Qureshi
,
2024 ONCA 131
at para.
26
.

[
36
]

The Crown submits that I should reject Mr. Johnson's evidence,
arguing that he was not a credible witness. It argues that the inevitable
inference from the credible and reliable evidence is that Mr. Johnson intended
to drive at Mr. Babili, thereby intending to strike or threaten to strike him,
knowing that it would cause him to believe he would be struck. On the second
count, the Crown argues that on the basis of the witnesses and the videos, Mr.
Johnson's driving was objectively dangerous and represented a marked departure
from the standard of care of a reasonable driver.

Legal Analysis

Onus and Standard of Proof

[
37
]

I want to emphasize at the outset of my analysis that Mr. Johnson is
not on trial for having poor anger management skills or being obnoxious. For
that matter, he is not on trial for engaging in racist or bullying behavior. While
public controversy over the events in the state of Israel and its occupied
territories, especially Gaza, since October 7, 2023, are obviously background
to what happened here, this case is not about that controversy. Everyone in
Canada has the guaranteed freedom to peacefully assemble to express their
perspective, and all are entitled to be protected against non-peaceful
interferences with that expression. So, this is not a case about that conflict.

[
38
]

Mr. Johnson's words were, by his own admission, intended to provoke.
They cannot be characterized as a reasoned intervention into an emotional and
divisive debate, but that also is not relevant. Just as the merits of Mr.
Johnson's political beliefs, whether about the Israel-Palestine conflict or
anything else, are completely irrelevant, so too is whether he expressed them
appropriately.

[
39
]

What matters are Mr. Johnson's actions with his car and his intent
behind those actions. The offenses Mr. Johnson is charged with are, one,
allegedly using or threatening to use a weapon in committing assault of Omar
Babili and, two, operating a conveyance, i.e. his car, in a manner that, having
regard to all the circumstances, was dangerous to the public. The question I
therefore have to decide is whether the Crown has proven neither, one, or both
of these charges.

[
40
]

Any answer to this question begins with the principle set out in s.
11(d) of the
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
, namely that a person who is
charged with an offence has the right to be presumed innocent until proven
guilty. In the context of a criminal trial, that means the accused cannot be found
guilty unless the Crown proves every element of the offence beyond a reasonable
doubt.

[
41
]

In
R. v. Lifchus
,
1997 CanLII 319 (SCC)
, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 320 at para.
36
, Justice
Cory summarized the principle of proof beyond a reasonable doubt as follows:

a)         the standard of proof beyond a
reasonable doubt is inextricably intertwined with the presumption of innocence;

b)         the burden of proof rests on the prosecution throughout
the trial and never shifts to the accused;

c)         a reasonable doubt is not a doubt based upon sympathy or
prejudice;

d)         rather, a reasonable doubt is one based upon reason and
common sense;

e)         a reasonable doubt is logically connected to the evidence
or absence of evidence;

f)          proof beyond a reasonable doubt does not involve proof
to an absolute certainty; it is not proof beyond
any
doubt nor is it an
imaginary or frivolous doubt; it is however closer to absolute certainty than
to a balance of probabilities; and

g)         more is required than proof that the accused is probably
guilty — a trier of fact concluding only that the accused is probably guilty
must acquit.

[
42
]

Where, as here, an accused person gives evidence
in their own defence, the trier of fact must embark
upon the analysis set out at in
R. v. W.(D.)
,
1991 CanLII 93 (SCC)
, [1991] 1 S.C.R. 742 at pp.
757–58. In
W.(D.)
, Justice Cory, on behalf of the Supreme Court of
Canada, approved the following jury charge in circumstances where the
complainant testified that a sexual assault had occurred and the accused denied
it:

First, if you
believe the evidence of the accused, obviously you must acquit.

Second, if you do not believe the testimony
of the accused but you are left in reasonable doubt by it, you must acquit.

Third, even if
you are not left in doubt by the evidence of the accused, you must ask yourself
whether, on the basis of the evidence which you do accept, you are convinced
beyond a reasonable doubt by that evidence of the guilt of the accused.

[
43
]

In
R. v. H.(C.W.)
(1991),
1991 CanLII
3956 (BC CA)
, 68 C.C.C. (3d) 146 at p. 155 (B.C.C.A.), the Court of Appeal
added the following question, after the second question in
W.(D.)
:

If, after a
careful consideration of all of the evidence, you are unable to decide whom to
believe, you must acquit.

[
44
]

The
W.(D.)
test, as modified by
H. (C.W.)

was summarized in
R. v. Ay
(1994),
1994 CanLII 8749 (BC CA)
, 93 C.C.C.
(3d) 456 at pp. 476–77 as follows:

(a)        If
the trier of fact believes the accused [with respect to their exculpatory
evidence], they must acquit.

(b)        If
the trier of fact does not know whether to believe the accused, they must
acquit.

(c)        If
the trier of fact does not reject the evidence of the accused they will have a
reasonable doubt and must acquit.

(d)        If the trier
of fact disbelieves the accused, that is if they reject his or her evidence as
untrue, they have to be convinced beyond a reasonable doubt of the guilt of the
accused on the whole of the evidence before they could convict.

[
45
]

The ultimate question for the trier of fact is whether, on all of
the evidence, they are left with a reasonable doubt as to the accused’s guilt.
A lack of credibility on the part of the accused does not equate to proof of
guilt beyond a reasonable doubt:
R. v. D.J.M.
,
2021 BCSC 1024
at para.
42
.

[
46
]

Although it is not strictly necessary to organize analysis of the
evidence in this fashion, it is often helpful to consider the evidence of the
accused (and any other exculpatory evidence)
first
to consider whether
the trier of fact believes it, does not know whether to believe it or conclude
that they cannot “reject it” (i.e. it raises a reasonable doubt). Then, and
only if the evidence of the accused and the exculpatory evidence does not raise
a reasonable doubt, the trier of fact should separately consider the
inculpatory evidence (the “Crown’s case”) to see if it is convincing beyond a
reasonable doubt. I will follow this approach.

[
47
]

To be sure, the reliability and credibility of any evidence depends
at least in part in comparing it with the circumstance of the case in the whole.
For that reason, when I consider whether I can reject Mr. Johnson's evidence, I
can, and indeed must, consider the evidence relied on by the Crown:
R. v. Redden
,

2021 BCCA 230
, at para.
80
. But at that stage I will only do so for the purposes
of assessing whether the exculpatory evidence raises a reasonable doubt, or
equivalently, assessing whether I believe it, do not know whether to believe
it, or cannot reject it.

Elements of the Offences Charged

[
48
]

On the first count of the indictment, Mr. Johnson is charged under
s.
267
(a) of the
Criminal
Code
, which makes it an indictable offence
per person to, in committing an assault, carry, use, or threaten to use a “weapon”
or an imitation thereof. The offence is conveniently referred to as “assault with
a weapon”.

[
49
]

The elements of “assault with a weapon” include all the elements of
common assault, but add the elements of, in this case, threatening to use or
using a weapon in the course of the assault:
R. v. M.S. B.
,
2021 BCPC
337
at para.
47–48
. (Carrying is not applicable here because it is not in the
indictment and does not arise on the facts.) The elements of using or
threatening to use a weapon must coincide in time with the elements of the
common assault.

[
50
]

Assault is defined in s. 265 of the
Code
.
The relevant form of assault is defined at s. 265(1)(b) as follows:

A person commits an assault when

[...]

(b)        he attempts or
threatens, by an act or a gesture, to apply force to another person, if he has,
or causes the other person to believe on reasonable grounds that he has,
present ability to effect his purpose.

[
51
]

“Attempts or threatens” is disjunctive. The Crown can thus establish
an assault either by showing that the accused attempted, by an act or a
gesture, to apply force to the complainant or by showing that the accused
threatened to apply force.

[
52
]

“Attempt” is a defined term in the
Criminal
Code
.
Section 24(1)
says:

24(1)    Every
one who, having an intent to commit an offence, does or omits to do anything
for the purpose of carrying out the intention is guilty of an attempt to commit
the offence whether or not it was possible under the circumstances to commit
the offence.

[
53
]

The distinction between “preparation” and “attempt” is a question of
law according to s. 24(2) of the
Code
. It raises difficult questions in
some cases. But in this case, it is clear that if Mr. Johnson had a criminal
intent in making the Sudden Left Turn, he clearly went beyond mere
“preparation”, so no difficult distinction between preparation and attempt
could arise on these facts.

[
54
]

The key question here is whether Mr. Johnson, in making the Sudden
Left Turn, had the “intent” to apply force to Mr. Babili: if he did, the Sudden
Left Turn would be an “attempt”; if he did not intend to apply force, it would
not be an attempt, and thus an assault could only be made out on the “threat”
branch. In my analysis, I will therefore not consider the preparation/attempt
distinction and will focus on what the Crown has proven about Mr. Johnson’s
intent to have his car hit Mr. Babili.

[
55
]

The “threat” branch of s. 265(1)(b) also requires analysis. Unlike
the word “attempt”, the word “threat” is not generally defined in the
Code
.

[
56
]

There is an imperfect analogy between threatening words and
threatening acts or gestures. Both involve an objective sense of “threat”
(i.e., whether the act creates a risk of harm) and a subjective sense (i.e.,
whether the person engaging in the act intends someone else to experience that
risk of harm). As a basic principle of criminal law, both must come together for
the offence to be made out.

[
57
]

In the context of “uttering threats”, the
actus reus
is made
out if a reasonable person aware of the circumstances in which the words were
uttered would have perceived them to be a threat and the
mens rea
is
made out if the accused intended to intimidate or have the words taken
seriously:
R. v. McRae
,
2013 SCC 68
at paras.
10–23
.

[
58
]

By analogy, in the context of threatening acts, the
actus reus

would be made out if a reasonable person would find the act to pose the risk
that it would result in the application of force, while the
mens rea
would
only be made out if the accused formed an intention to intimidate or wanted a
person to believe that force would be applied.

[
59
]

In the context of Mr. Johnson’s Sudden Left Turn into the driveway
where Mr. Babili was, the Crown can therefore establish an assault by
showing that Mr. Babili or someone in his circumstances would reasonably
perceive a risk of force being applied if it can also show that Mr. Johnson
intended Mr. Babili to perceive that risk.

[
60
]

To establish an assault with a weapon, the Crown
will also have to show that the car was a weapon at the relevant time. “Weapon”
is defined in s. 2 of the
Code
to be:

any thing used, designed to be used or
intended for use

(a)        in causing death or injury to any
person, or

(b)        for
the purpose of threatening or intimidating any person.

[
61
]

The car was a “weapon” if, but only if, the Crown can show, beyond a
reasonable doubt, that Mr. Johnson used it for the purpose of threatening or
intimidating Mr. Babili. This requires the Crown to establish both the use of
the car (which is not contested) and that this use was intended to be used in
causing injury to Mr. Babili or for the purpose of threatening or intimidating
Mr. Babili.

[
62
]

This analysis of whether the car was a weapon parallels the two
kinds of intention that could establish assault. If the Crown can prove Mr.
Johnson intended to hit Mr. Babili, and thereby cause him injury, that would
make the car a weapon. Alternatively, if the Crown can prove Mr. Johnson
intended to threaten or intimidate Mr. Babili by scaring him and forcing him to
get out of the way, that would also make the car a weapon, even if Mr. Johnson
did not intend to actually hit him.

[
63
]

There was some argument before me as to whether Mr. Johnson could
have committed assault with a weapon if he intended to scare, but not hit, Mr.
Babili. In my view, the case law provided to me supports the principle that
this is one of the ways his actions could constitute an assault and his car
could constitute a weapon.

[
64
]

Mr. Firestone referred me to
R. v. Gill
,
2014 BCPC 105
[
Gill
]
and
R. v. M.S.B.
,
2021 BCPC 337
[
M.S.B.
].

[
65
]

In
Gill
, the accused had a motor vehicle accident with her
ex-husband. The judge found no evidence that she had done so “deliberately”
(which, in context, I take to be synonymous with “intentionally” and not
necessarily to imply deliberation). The accused was therefore acquitted of
assault with a weapon (and of dangerous driving, which I will address later).

[
66
]

Gill
establishes that an accidental motor
vehicle collision cannot constitute assault or assault with a weapon. On the
facts of
Gill
, the possibility that the accused meant to threaten or
intimidate the complainant, but not hit him, did not arise.

[
67
]

In
M.S.B.
, in the course of leaving the family home as a
result of a marital dispute, the accused grabbed a baby gate and threw it.
There was a dispute on the facts about where the accused was standing and where
the gate was thrown. The Crown alleged that the accused knew where the
complainant was standing and threw the gate at her, but this was not proven
beyond a reasonable doubt.

[
68
]

In
M.S.B.
, Judge Chettiar referred to the decision of the
Manitoba Court of Appeal in
R. v. Vandergraaf
(1994),
1994 CanLII 16617 (MB CA)
, 93 C.C.C. (3d)
286, in which that court overturned the assault-with-a-weapon conviction of a
hockey fan who attempted to throw a jar of peanut butter at the hockey rink
surface and instead struck and injured the complainant.

[
69
]

In
Vandergraaf
, the Court stated:

Without proof of
an intention to apply force to the complainant or to another person, there
cannot be a conviction for an assault, or as charged in this case, a conviction
under [what was then] s. 267(1)(a) of [the]
Criminal Code
of an assault with a
weapon.

[
70
]

Parsed as if it were a statutory text, this statement in
Vandergraaf

might imply that the
only
way the element of assault can be made out is
if a person intends to apply force, which may not be the case if a person
threatens to apply force, but does not really intend to follow through on that
threat. A person has an intention to threaten if, by an act or gesture, in
circumstances in which the person doing the threatening either has or causes
the other person to believe that they have, the present ability to effect their
purpose, but such a person may not have “an intention to apply force to the
complainant or to another person.”

[
71
]

However, this is not the correct way to read statements by appellate
courts. In the factual circumstances of
Vandergraaf
, the Manitoba Court
of Appeal’s statement made sense. There was no air of reality to a Crown theory
that the accused was threatening anyone nor does that theory appear to have
been advanced. In context, the point the Manitoba Court of Appeal was making
was that throwing a jar of peanut butter, even negligently and inappropriately,
is not an assault just because it hit someone. I do not take the court in
Vandergraaf

to have been denying that an intention to threaten could ever be the requisite
mental element of an assault or an assault with a weapon.

[
72
]

The Crown relies on
R. v. Dawydiuk
,
2010 BCCA 162
.
Dawydiuk

considered an appeal in which the accused drove his truck on to the sidewalk
outside a bar and hit a female bar patron. The accused’s defence was that he
drove onto the sidewalk out of necessity to avoid being attacked. The trial
judge rejected the accused’s testimony, but also rejected the only Crown
evidence that the accused intended to hit someone. Rather, the trial judge
found that the accused “threatened to apply force to another person.” The Court
of Appeal upheld his conviction.

[
73
]

In
Dawydiuk
at paras.
31–32
, the Court of Appeal stated that
the Crown was not required to prove that the accused intended to hit the
complainant. It was enough that the accused had threatened to apply force to
those on the sidewalk though his acts. This intention could be inferred from
circumstantial evidence, although of course only if the principles applying to
the use of circumstantial evidence in criminal cases apply.

[
74
]

In light of the provisions of the
Criminal Code
specifying
the offence under
s. 267
(a) and defining “assault” and “weapon”, as
authoritatively interpreted in
Dawydiuk
, I instruct myself that in order
to convict Mr. Johnson of that offence, I must find that the Crown has proven
the following beyond a reasonable doubt:

a)         That the Sudden Left Turn was an “act”. I will not
analyze this at length, since this does not appear to be in dispute and is in
any event obvious.

b)         That Mr. Johnson, in making the Sudden Left Turn, was
either attempting or threatening to apply force to Mr. Babili.

i.          For the Sudden Left Turn to be an attempt to apply
force, the Crown must establish both that it went beyond mere preparation to
apply force to Mr. Babili or another person and that Mr. Johnson intended
to apply force to Mr. Babili. I will not analyze the element of “going beyond
mere preparation” at length because if Mr. Johnson intended to apply force to
Mr. Babili, then there is no air of reality to the proposition that the
Sudden Left Turn did not go beyond mere preparation. However, the issue of
whether Mr. Johnson intended to apply force to Mr. Babili is obviously at the
core of the case and I will analyze at length whether the evidence sustains a
finding, beyond a reasonable doubt, that Mr. Johnson had that intention.

ii.         For the Sudden Left Turn to be a threat to apply force,
the Crown must establish both that a reasonable person would perceive the risk
that force would be applied to Mr. Babili and that Mr. Johnson intended to
intimidate Mr. Babili or to have him believe that force would be applied to
him. Again, I do not intend to analyze the
actus reus
at length here
because it is very clear from the videos that a reasonable person would
perceive a risk that Mr. Babili would be hit and that Mr. Babili in fact did
perceive that risk. I have no evidence that would raise an air of reality to
the contrary proposition. However, the existence of an intention on Mr.
Johnson’s part either to intimidate Mr. Babili or have him believe that he
would be hit is very much in issue, and I will analyze the evidence at length
on this score to determine whether this element has been proven beyond a
reasonable doubt.

c)         That Mr. Johnson, when making the left turn, had or
caused Mr. Babili on reasonable grounds to believe that he had, the ability to
effect a purpose of applying force to Mr. Babili with the car. As the driver of
a car facing a pedestrian in a driveway, Mr. Johnson clearly had that ability
to effect the purpose of applying force. Mr. Babili’s unchallenged evidence was
that he believed that Mr. Johnson could hit him with the car and this was
clearly reasonable in the circumstances. I will not analyze this element
further.

d)         That Mr. Johnson used his car with intention of causing
injury to Mr. Babili or for the purpose of threatening or intimidating Mr.
Babili. This element is necessary for the car to have been a “weapon”. In the
specific circumstances of this case, this element is also necessary to
establish assault. I will therefore analyze the evidence in relation to
intention together, noting that if it is proven beyond a reasonable doubt, the
offence under s. 267(a) of the
Code
is made out.

Analysis of Exculpatory Evidence

[
75
]

In his testimony, Mr. Johnson denied he was trying to hit Mr. Babili
when he executed the Sudden Left Turn. When asked, point blank, on direct,
whether he was trying to hit Mr. Babili, he responded “No, 100 percent no.”

[
76
]

Under the
W.(D.)

principle, I must acquit Mr. Johnson of the
intention‑to‑apply-force

branch of assault if I believe, do not know whether to believe, or do not
reject ,Mr. Johnson's exculpatory testimony in this regard. Since it is not the
kind of thing Mr. Johnson could plausibly misremember or misperceive, this is a
question of Mr. Johnson's credibility in the narrow sense of his truthfulness,
not his reliability.

[
77
]

The Crown argues that Mr. Johnson is not a credible witness, saying
he was evasive, unresponsive, not candid, and made statements that were
unreasonable in light of internal and external inconsistencies. On behalf of
Mr. Johnson, Mr. Firestone points out that Mr. Johnson was candid about
matters that did not paint him in a good light and submits that I should accept
his evidence as credible overall.

[
78
]

I have concerns about Mr. Johnson's credibility. For example, in
direct examination, Mr. Johnson said he made eye contact with Mr. Babili before
making his Sudden Left Turn and that Mr. Babili was wearing a reflective vest. He
testified that he saw Mr. Babili running once he began the turn, although he
remembered him running north, as opposed to the southerly direction the videos
show. However, in cross-examination, he claimed he did not see Mr. Babili while
turning because he was looking through his window rather than his windshield. This
is not consistent with common sense, with Mr. Babili's testimony or with his own
observation that he thought Mr. Babili was going northward. I find that there
is simply no way he could have not seen Mr. Babili, when he made his turn.

[
79
]

Also, in the course of cross-examination, Mr. Johnson claimed that
he thought Mr. Babili was motioning him to make the turn.

[
80
]

THE SHERIFF:  No, no, you can't go.

[
81
]

THE COURT:  Mr. Johnson, you cannot go. You have to stay in this courtroom.

[
82
]

THE ACCUSED:  Do you realize what you're saying?

[
83
]

THE COURT:  Mr. Johnson, if you do not remain quiet and stay where
you are, you are going to have to go into the box. Do you understand me?

[
84
]

THE ACCUSED:  Sure. Thank you.

[
85
]

THE COURT:  Thank you. I will resume.

[
86
]

Also, in the course of cross-examination, Mr. Johnson claimed that
he thought Mr. Babili was motioning him to make the turn. Nothing in the video
or in the evidence of any of the other eye witnesses supports this statement. He
did not make the claim in his direct examination, though it would have been a
natural part of his narrative if it were true. His demeanor while making this
claim was different than in other more plausible parts of his testimony. He
seemed sarcastic and insouciant when he said this. I conclude that the claim
was false and knowingly so.

[
87
]

Since I cannot help but conclude that the claim that Mr. Johnson
thought Mr. Babili was directing him to make the turn was fabrication, this
colours Mr. Johnson's credibility generally.

[
88
]

With that exception, though, what Mr. Johnson did when he did not
want to concede something or when he found an area — something that was not
good for him — he did not directly fabricate, but would be evasive when he did not
want to answer something.

[
89
]

I regard Mr. Johnson's testimony with caution, but I cannot reject
all of it. In particular, I do not reject his denial that he intended to hit
Mr. Babili, and so I am left in a reasonable doubt with respect to whether he
intended to do so. His testimony that he did not intend to actually hit Mr.
Babili is supported, to some extent, by the video evidence that while he
accelerated when first making the turn, he braked and came to rest with part of
his car still on the sidewalk and part of his car still out into the road. This
is consistent with a desire to scare Mr. Babili without actually hitting him.

[
90
]

Moreover, there was a distinction in Mr. Johnson's demeanor when he
denied wanting to hit Mr. Babili's with his demeanor when making the claims
that I reject. I do not want to put too much weight on the demeanor, but my
impression is that while Mr. Johnson was not entirely truthful, he is not a
smooth liar, either, and I could generally see a difference in the way he spoke
when he was being evasive, forthright or making something up.

[
91
]

With respect to questions about whether he intended to
scare

Mr. Babili, Mr. Johnson was generally evasive.

[
92
]

In the course of cross-examination admitted that if Mr. Babili had
not moved, he would have been where Mr. Johnson's car stopped and therefore
would have been hit. He said in justification of this that he thought Mr. Babili
must have been a soccer player. This seems been based on racial stereotypes in
his own mind about men of Arab or Middle Eastern ethnicity.

[
93
]

As I will go on to explain, this is quite inculpatory evidence in
terms of whether Mr. Johnson had the intention of intimidating or threatening
Mr. Babili. However, it is consistent with, in his own mind, trying to drive in
such a way that Mr. Babili would not in fact be hit. Within his own distorted thinking,
he may well have hoped and expected that Mr. Babili would get out of the way. And
therefore, I have, at minimum, a reasonable doubt as to whether Mr. Johnson
intended to actually apply force to Mr. Babili.

[
94
]

In this respect, the guidance in the Supreme Court of Canada in
W.(D.)

is
critical. It would not be enough for me to conclude that Mr. Johnson was
probably lying when he denied intending to hit Mr. Babili. If I cannot reject
Mr. Johnson's testimony in this regard, I cannot convince him based on attempt
theory of assault or of his car being a weapon. Since I cannot reject Mr.
Johnson's evidence that he did not intend to hit Mr. Babili, I would therefore
not convict him on that basis.

[
95
]

That, of course, does not mean he could not be
convicted of assault with a weapon on the alternative basis of intention to threaten
or intimidate, which I will now address.

[
96
]

I find that Mr. Johnson's exculpatory evidence
on this question, such as it was, was highly evasive. And this was a contrast
to his firm answers on whether he intended to hit Mr. Babili. On my review, Mr.
Johnson did not give clear exculpatory evidence about an intention to scare or
intimidate Mr. Babili, in his direct examination. He gave some such evidence in
cross-examination, but reluctantly and evasively.

[
97
]

His initial narrative of the Sudden Left Turn was
as follows:

I saw a fellow with a reflective vest on,
and he would appear to have one of those tiny flags you see at a sports match
or something. He was in the middle of the road, making eye contact with me. I
was already cognizant of the fact that there were people behind me, and that
was when I made the decision to turn into the driveway.

[Question:] Describe what you did.

I turned hard left, but I braked before the
entrance to the driveway.

[Question:] Why did you do that?

Because I was upset. I was already yelling,
so I was heavy on the acceleration.

[Question:] For what purpose?

To get out — to
speaking with Abou Said, to tell him what was what.

[
98
]

Despite Mr. Firestone's able argument, I do not accept that the
final answer is exculpatory as to Mr. Johnson’s intentions. It identifies the
purpose of the Sudden Left Turn as to get out to continue arguing with Mr. Abou
Said. That would only be exculpatory if the intention to park in order to
confront Mr. Abou Said was incompatible with also having the intention to
scare, intimidate, or threaten Mr. Babili. But these are not incompatible
intentions.

[
99
]

The fact that Mr. Johnson confronted Mr. Abou Said rather than chase
after Mr. Babili is evidence of a lack of
individual
animus toward Mr. Babili,
but that is not the point. Mr. Johnson's animus on this evidence was not
towards any individual protester, but to the pro-Palestinian protesters in
general. It is important to note that Mr. Johnson knew neither of these individuals,
and his only reason for anger against them was the cause that they were
promoting. They were thus interchangeable targets of his ire from his
perspective.

[
100
]

When asked about his speed, Mr. Johnson said the following, “The
initial acceleration may be 50 kilometers an hour, but it was short-lived
succession — acceleration, before I hit the brakes.” Mr. Johnson was asked
whether the left turn had anything to do with Mr. Babili and responded as
follows, “Uh, subconsciously, I actually thought there was a level of
stewardship in regard to traffic.” This was obviously a
non-sequitur
.

[
101
]

Mr. Firestone asked him again, as follows:

[Question:] I ask you specifically, did you
aim at him?

No.

[Question:] Were you trying to hit him?

No, 100 percent no.

[Question:] Was he even your focus when you
made that left turn?

Answer: One
hundred percent not. My focus was to get out and tell Abou Said what was what.

[
102
]

This is a clear denial that Mr. Johnson intended to hit Babili, but
it is evasive on the subject of whether he was trying to threaten or intimidate
Mr. Babili, at best equivocal on that subject. While Mr. Johnson said his focus
was not on Mr. Babili, in this answer, he subsequently denied that his focus
was on Mr. Abou Said while he was driving, saying it was on the turn. And then
when asked again whether his focus was on Mr. Babili, he said, “No, except out
of the corner of my eye.”

[
103
]

These are obviously internal inconsistencies, in what is at most an equivocal
denial that he “had a focus on” Mr. Babili. In any event, denying that he had a
“focus on” Mr. Babili, as opposed to Mr. Abou Said, is not a denial that he
intended to scare a protester.

[
104
]

I should say that even if I take this as a denial that he had any
intention of scaring Mr. Babili, which it does not really appear to be, I would
not find the denial credible. First, it is an odd way of making such a claim when
a straightforward denial that he intended to scare Mr. Babili was available.

[
105
]

Second, it is not believable that none of Mr. Johnson's focus, when
he was executing a driving maneuver, and from the perspective of driving, he
did so with control and quite skillfully, was on the individual right in front
of him, with whom he had just had eye contact and who was wearing a bright vest.

[
106
]

From Mr. Johnson's perspective, both Mr. Abou Said and Mr. Babili
were just pro-Palestinian protesters who appeared to be of Arab ethnic background.
There was nothing individual about either of them, so far as he was concerned. His
animosity was a generalized one, not about either of these specific individuals.
Therefore, even if Mr. Johnson's claim about his focus on Mr. Abou Said could
be taken to be a denial of any intention to scare Mr. Babili, which I do not
find, it would not be of sufficient credibility to raise a reasonable doubt.

[
107
]

Indeed, while Mr. Johnson quite clearly denied trying to hit Mr.
Babili in direct examination before taking the videos, he said a number of
things that could be taken as admissions that he intended to scare Mr. Babili.

[
108
]

Mr. Johnson, in direct, recalled saying “This is
the sort of things that happen to Jews all the time, in Israel.” In what is
clearly a reference to the statement is recorded in — by Video 1 as, “This is
what” either you or they “are doing to the Jews, all the time.” Asked about
whether any of the statements were in respect of Mr. Babili, Mr. Johnson
responded as follows:

The fact that my car came within a metre or
so of him, that statement that I just made, my intention with what I said, that
was in regard to the fellow in the safety vest, not in regard to Abou Said.

Because I
realized he [i.e., the person in the safety vest] was within a metre or so when
I turned in, and so I said this is the kind of thing that happens to Jews all
the time, at the hands of people with opposing [inaudible, possibly “views”].

[
109
]

This is an admission. Mr. Johnson equated terrorism by Palestinian
organizations against Jews in Israel to his almost hitting Mr. Babili, seconds
before. The only possible meaning is that these were both acts intended to
scare people to advance a political cause. There is no air of reality to the
proposition of what Mr. Johnson meant by “what was happening to Jews all
the time” was accidental bad driving. It must have been a reference to violence
or terrorism. Mr. Johnson was clearly saying he intended to scare Mr. Babili,
analogously to how Jews or Israelis are terrorized by violence from Hamas or
other Palestinian organizations.

[
110
]

After giving this answer, Mr. Johnson denied that he was trying to
strike anybody. He said that during the Sudden Left Turn his car was “under
control”. He did not, however, say he did not intend to scare Mr. Babili at
that point, despite the fact that this was an opportune time to do so. I think
that is telling. Mr. Johnson felt he could scare Mr. Babili without actually
hitting him, and this would have (from his perspective) a beneficial impact on
the protesters of scaring them.

[
111
]

The subject was returned to while Mr. Johnson
was reviewing Video 3. Mr. Johnson testified he saw Mr. Babili walking
straight for him and made eye contact with him.

Q. [At 44 s. on Video 3]. Can you tell me
whether or not at any time your focus moved away from Mr. Abou Said up to the
point you made this left hand turn.

A. No, I was still I am thinking I was still
going, to be honest. I just remember turning and I thought buddy [i.e., Mr.
Babili] went to the other, opposite direction.

Q. You are saying that is your memory.

A. Yes, I stated that earlier. I said when I
turned in I thought he ran south, not north.

Q. [48 s.] When you made that left hand
turn, were you driving at the person in the vest.

A. 100% not.

Q. 100% not?

A. Yes.

[
112
]

Although it is still somewhat equivocal, I accept the interpretation
that this final denial was a denial that he was driving in Mr. Babili’s
direction, including with an intent to hit or scare him. However, the video
makes it extremely clear that Mr. Johnson was in fact driving at Mr.
Babili.

[
113
]

I cannot find Mr. Johnson’s evidence on this score would raise a
reasonable doubt, on its own, or in conjunction with other answers, both
because of the internal inconsistencies I referred to, but also because the
objective evidence makes it clear that the car was going in the direction of
the person in the vest, i.e. Mr. Babili.

[
114
]

As I have noted, the evidence was that Mr. Babili was right in front
of Mr. Johnson with an unobscured view, in a safety vest. And finally,
fundamentally undermining the credibility of this answer, if it is interpreted
as a denial of trying to scare Mr. Babili, was the fact that the video shows at
the very last minute, or last second, rather, that Mr. Johnson cuts in further
to the left with his vehicle, which is precisely in the direction where Mr.
Babili is.

[
115
]

I note that Mr. Johnson, in his testimony, said he made a turn as
close to 90 percent as physically possible. And the only reason to have
done it would be to try to either hit or at least scare Mr. Babili.

[
116
]

I accept that Mr. Johnson testified in direct examination that after
he got out of his car, he did not pursue Mr. Babili on foot and instead decided
to confront Mr. Abou Said. This is clearly true, but it is consistent with
trying to intimidate Mr. Babili moments before, so I would not consider it
exculpatory evidence.

[
117
]

When it was first put to him by Crown counsel
that he intended to scare Mr. Babili, Mr. Johnson responded:

If people get
scared sometimes, and I have no control over it, that’s up to them how they
choose to respond. I am not responsible for every [inaudible]’s feelings or
emotions all the time.

[
118
]

This is an evasive answer to a direct question. A denial of
responsibility for Mr. Babili's fear is not the same as the denial of an
intention to produce it, which was the question put to him by Crown counsel.

[
119
]

I note that this answer represents blame-shifting, since Mr. Johnson
had at that point already acknowledged that Mr. Babili had no reason to expect
a Sudden Left Turn and had run to avoid being hit.

[
120
]

And when counsel for the Crown repeated the
suggestion that Mr. Johnson intended either to hit or scare Mr. Babili in
response to Mr. Babili waving Palestinian flag in his direction, Mr. Johnson
stated the following:

Q. Just seconds after he does that is when
you accelerated towards him.

A. No, I didn’t accelerate towards him.

Q. You don’t think this is accelerating
towards him.

A.
You
do.

Q. I suggest to you sir that when he waved
that flag at you that triggered you to come and either hit him or scare him by
being close to him.

A. Ok, you’re welcome
to do so.

[
121
]

This is a flippant answer and also an evasive one.

[
122
]

Further on in cross-examination, Mr. Johnson said things that
support the inference that he did in fact intend to make Mr. Babili scared he
would be hit, even if he did not intend to actually hit him:

a)         He admitted he knew he came very close to Mr. Babili with
his car and that he knew he had done so when he engaged in his second
confrontation with Mr. Abou Said.

b)         In response to suggestion that he was, “proud of almost
hitting Mr. Babili,” he responded as follows. “I was proud of the fact
that I was helping them have empathy with the Jews they were taught to hate,
maybe since they were babies.” The only reasonable interpretation of that is
that he was intending to cause them, which in this context must have meant the
protesters, to have empathy by being scared of an act of violence.

[
123
]

At the very end of the cross‑examination, Mr. Johnson did deny
he intended either to hit Mr. Babili or, “come close to him.” However, he had
already admitted that he did, in fact, come close to him and he was in control
of his vehicle at all times. So, there is an internal inconsistency there.

[
124
]

Mr. Johnston did deny that he made his comments comparing what he
had just done with his car with respect to Mr. Babili to what was being done to
Jews. But he did say he wanted Mr. Abou Said to believe he intended to target
Mr. Babili. Put to him point blank that his purpose was to intimidate Mr. Babili,
he denied that, but there is no other rational explanation.

[
125
]

Mr. Johnson gave one answer that suggests he knew Mr. Babili was frightened.
In the context of being asked about his moment of eye contact with Mr. Babili,
Mr. Johnson said the following, “He was in the middle of the road and I saw
this little flag, but I saw his eyes more than anything, and he looked
concerned.” This statement about Mr. Babili looking concerned, as an
observation of something that occurred before the Left Turn, does not make much
sense. Rather, Mr. Johnson recalling seeing what he characterized as concern in
Mr. Babili's eyes, makes more sense as a realization that he frightened Mr.
Babili. This implies at least reckless indifference as to Mr. Babili's being
scared because of his driving, an indifference Mr. Johnson repeated when he
said he was not responsible for Mr. Babili's emotional state.

[
126
]

So as a result of this foregoing analysis, I do not find that Mr.
Johnson's testimony can give rise to a reasonable doubt as to whether he
intended to threaten Mr. Babili.

[
127
]

Under the
W.(D.)

analysis, though, that is not the end of the story.
Even if I have rejected Mr. Johnson’s evidence as lacking sufficient
credibility to raise a reasonable doubt on that score, I must consider the Crown
case in its totality. I will do so briefly, because I have addressed some of
those issues already.

[
128
]

I am satisfied that the inculpatory evidence in its totality can
only give rise to the only reasonable inference is that Mr. Johnson did intend
to at least intimidate Mr. Babili.

[
129
]

First of all is the basic inference that adults of ordinary capacity
intend the natural consequences of their acts. Mr. Johnson testified that he
made eye contact with Mr. Babili, when Mr. Babili waved his flag. Specifically,
he said he noticed the look of concern in Mr. Babili's eyes. He then made the Sudden
Left Turn, which of course scared Mr. Babili. Mr. Babili was right in front of
him, wearing a reflective safety vest. Mr. Johnson had control of the car,
throughout. Mr. Johnson conceded he saw Mr. Babili trying to run, although he
remembers this occurring in the opposite direction that it in fact did.

[
130
]

In my view, it is contrary to ordinary human experience and common
sense that these results would not have been intended by Mr. Johnson in the
circumstances, so in particular, that Mr. Babili's fleeing would not have been
intended by Mr. Johnson, in the circumstances.

[
131
]

Second is Mr. Johnson's inculpatory statement that he believed Mr.
Babili to be a soccer player, during cross-examination. This only makes sense
if he thought he was justified in moving his car to where Mr. Babili was
located because Mr. Babili could get out of the way fast. In addition to being
a racial stereotype, this is a thought that would only occur to him if Mr.
Johnson intended to give Mr. Babili a scare but did not want to actually hit
him.

[
132
]

Third, Video 3 shows not just that Mr. Johnson made an extremely
sharp turn, as confirmed by Mr. Johnson's testimony, but also that he turned
even
further
to the left, or north, at the last instant, just as Mr. Babili is
escaping in that direction. The car then comes to rest, occupying part of the
crosswalk, which Mr. Johnson had no other reason to want to do. These
circumstances are not explained by Mr. Johnson, and not consistently explain
the thought Mr. Johnson — that Mr. Babili was escaping southward. That may be
his memory, but it could not have been his perception at the time.

[
133
]

Fourth, Mr. Johnson's equivocal claims that he did not intend to
scare Mr. Babili are not consistent with his own explanation of what he
meant by comparing what had just happened to what Jews experience in Israel. This
is clearly not a reference to accidental driving. It is clearly a reference to
acts intended to create fear.

[
134
]

Mr. Johnson hinted at an explanation that the “lesson” derived from
a “messy situation” and attempted to suggest that that might have been trying
to say there should be a lesson drawn from an accident. He did not state that
clearly, but in any event, I cannot find that that is a reasonable inference from
the proven fact of what he said. The only rational reference is that by referring
to what Jews experience in Israel, what he was referring to was intentional acts
designed to create, at minimum, fear.

[
135
]

If Mr. Johnson's testimony that the Sudden Left Turn was motivated
by concern about the traffic behind him, is taken to be exculpatory, I reject
it. There was nothing about the sequence of events that suggests that there was
a particular moment that he would have become particularly concerned about the
traffic behind him, which he had been blocking for a while. In fact, Video 2
shows that Mr. Johnson made the left turn in front of an oncoming vehicle,
which is not what a driver motivated by ordinary traffic considerations would
do. They would wait for that vehicle to pass and then make a left turn. Or Mr.
Johnson could have gone right onto Quebec Street, which was his original
destination.

[
136
]

I accept that the only direct evidence regarding Mr. Johnson's
intention was Mr. Johnson's, which I have rejected. The Crown's case that Mr.
Johnson intended to threaten Mr. Babili is necessary circumstantial, but as
Dawydiuk

establishes, this does not necessarily mean that the Crown will not succeed in
establishing his intention from his actions in the car.

[
137
]

Where the Crown's case rests on circumstantial evidence, the trier
of fact must be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the guilt of the
accused is the only reasonable inference to be drawn from the established facts.
However, in my view, taking together the established fact that Mr. Johnson's Sudden
Left Turn occurred immediately after he saw Mr. Babili waving the Palestinian flag,
second, that the resting point of the car was where Mr. Babili was one second
before, third, that Mr. Babili was directly in front of Mr. Johnson the entire
time, wearing a safety vest and clearly visible, fourth, that Mr. Johnson was
in control of this vehicle at all times, and taking into account the natural
inference that adults of full capacity intend the natural consequences of their
actions, I think the only reasonable explanation is that Mr. Johnson wanted to scare
a protester.

[
138
]

I do not doubt that Mr. Johnson also wanted to continue to target
Mr. Abou Said for argument, but I reject any contention that this desire was either
incompatible with intention to threaten or intimidate Mr. Babili.

[
139
]

The totality of the inculpatory evidence is overwhelming of an
intention to make Mr. Babili fear serious bodily harm in response to Mr. Babili
waving the Palestine flag and shouting “Free Palestine,” both of which triggered
animosity in Mr. Johnson, but both of which were Mr. Babili exercising his
constitutional rights of freedom of expression and peaceful assembly.

[
140
]

I find that the Crown has established that Mr. Johnson intended the natural
consequences of actions, in making the Sudden Left Turn, mainly causing Mr.
Babili to be frightened and have to run to avoid serious injury. Mr. Babili was
naturally frightened at the time and traumatized subsequently. Mr. Johnson, out
of anger, intended that a pro-Palestinian protester feel that way, because in
his own mind that was how Jews have been made to feel by Palestinian
organizations. That is the only reasonable explanation for his otherwise
inexplicable Sudden Left Turn. Any other explanation is fanciful and contrary
to any reasonable interpretation of the evidence. Since the other elements of
assault with a weapon have all been made out, I find that it is beyond a reasonable
doubt that Mr. Johnson assaulted Mr. Babili with his car and that it was in the
circumstances alleged.

“Dangerous Driving” Analysis

[
141
]

I will deal briefly with
s. 320.13(1)
of the
Criminal Code
,
which makes no defense for any person who operates a conveyance in the manner that,
having required all the circumstances, is dangerous to the public.

[
142
]

Section 320.13(1)
of the
Criminal Code
states
as follows:

Everyone commits
an offence who operates a conveyance in a manner that, having regard to all of
the circumstances, is dangerous to the public.

[
143
]

In
R. v. Hundal
,
1993 CanLII 120 (SCC)
, [1993] 1 S.C.R. 867,
the Supreme Court of Canada held that the “mental element” or “
mens rea
”
of this offence is determined through a “modified objective test”. The trier of
fact must be satisfied, beyond a reasonable doubt, that the objectively dangerous
conduct of the accused “amounted to a marked departure from the standard of
care that a reasonable person would observe in the accused's situation.” It is
not essential that the accused subjectively view their own conduct as
dangerous. As a general rule, personal factors will not be taken into account.
However, if an explanation is offered by the accused, such as a sudden and
unexpected onset of illness, then in order to convict, the trier of fact must
be satisfied that a reasonable person in similar circumstances ought to have
been aware of the risk and of the danger involved in the conduct manifested by
the accused.

[
144
]

Since
Hundal
, the Supreme Court of Canada has returned to the
“
mens rea
” element of this offence in
R. v. Beatty
,
2008 SCC 5
,
R.
v. Roy
,
2012 SCC 26
and
R. v. Chung
,
2020 SCC 8
. The facts of
these cases are as follows:

a)         In
Beatty
, the accused was driving properly prior
to suddenly, for no apparent reason, crossing the centre line into the path of
an oncoming vehicle, killing all three occupants. No intoxicants were involved.
The accused testified that he was not sure what happened, but he must have lost
consciousness or fallen asleep. The trial judge acquitted, and the Court of
Appeal reversed. The Supreme Court of Canada restored the acquittal.

b)         The trial in
Roy
occurred before the release of
the Supreme Court of Canada’s reasons in
Beatty
. The accident occurred
when visibility was limited due to fog. The accused was on an unpaved back
road. He stopped before entering onto the highway. He then proceeded, right
into the path of a tractor-trailer. In the resulting collision, a passenger was
killed. The trial judge convicted, and this conviction was upheld by the Court
of Appeal. The Supreme Court of Canada entered an acquittal.

c)         In
Chung
, the accused drove his vehicle at three
times the posted speed limit into the intersection of Oak Street and West 41
st

Avenue in Vancouver and collided with a left-turning vehicle. The trial judge
acquitted stating that while the driving was objectively dangerous, the
speeding was “momentary.” The Court of Appeal overturned the acquittal, and an
appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada was dismissed.

[
145
]

None of these cases purported to change the
Hundal
test of
“marked departure from the standard of care that a reasonable person would
observe in the accused's situation”. They did, however, elaborate it in the
following ways:

a)         In
Beatty
, the Supreme Court clarified that
personal characteristics of the accused are relevant if, but only if, they go
to the capacity of the accused to appreciate the risk or to avoid creating it.
If the accused has such capacity, their age, experience or education are not
relevant.

b)         In
Beatty
, the Supreme Court held that a
“deliberate intention” to create a danger would be suggestive of a marked
departure from the norm. However, dangerous conduct due to a “momentary lapse
of attention” will not generally constitute a marked departure from the norm.

c)         In
Roy
, the Court stated that the fault component
could be addressed with two questions:

i.          First, in light of all the relevant evidence, would a
reasonable person have foreseen the risk and taken steps to avoid it if at all
possible?

ii.         Second, was the accused’s failure to foresee the risk
and take possible steps to avoid it a marked departure from the standard of
care?

d)         In
Roy
, the Court emphasized the distinction
between a “marked” departure from the standard of care (necessary for dangerous
driving) and a “mere” departure (sufficient for civil liability in negligence).
This is a matter of degree, but a trial judge is under an obligation to
identify how and in what way the driver’s departure from the standard was
marked

as opposed to
mere
. Deliberately (or “intentionally”) creating a danger
would support a conviction, but is not required.

e)         In
Chung
, the Supreme Court held that an
overemphasis on the “momentariness” of the departure from the standard of care
in determining whether it is marked is an error of law. The reference to a
“momentary lapse of attention” in
Beatty
was interpreted as referring to
the “momentary mistakes that may be made by any reasonable driver”. The fact
that foreseeable consequences occur within a short period of time does not
preclude a finding of a marked departure from the standard of care.

[
146
]

Applying these principles here, I think there can be no reasonable
doubt that Mr. Johnson’s actions in the Sudden Left Turn were a marked
departure from the standard of care that a reasonable person would have
observed in his situation. No reasonable driver would suddenly turn into an
area of sidewalk occupied by a pedestrian, requiring that pedestrian to run
away to avoid being hit. If Mr. Johnson had not seen Mr. Babili, it would still
be a departure from the standard of care, but might possibly have been attributed
to the kind of momentary mistake an otherwise reasonable driver might make. But
the evidence, including Mr. Johnson’s evidence, is that he made eye contact
with Mr. Babili immediately before making the Sudden Left Turn. The videos,
especially Video 3, show Mr. Babili was in the line of his windshield directly
in front of where he was turning.

[
147
]

I reject Mr. Johnson’s suggestion in the course of cross-examination
that Mr. Babili waved him in or that he perceived that he waved him in, as
fabricated. This contradicts all the other evidence, including Video 3, and was
not stated in direct examination, although it would have been natural for Mr.
Johnson to do so if it had been true.

[
148
]

The Crown has established that Mr. Johnson intentionally created a
dangerous situation, which is sufficient for the mental element of dangerous
driving. I have no reasonable doubt about any of the elements of s. 320.13(1)
of the
Code
.

Conclusion and Order

[
149
]

Mr. Johnson, please stand.

[
150
]

On the first count of the indictment, which states that on or about

weapon, contrary to
s. 267
(a) of the
Criminal Code
, I find you
guilty.

[
151
]

On the second count of the indictment, which states that on or about
